planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed above 60°F; Sonja branches early from a low base, so give it more elbow room than single-stem types.

directions: Sow seed a half-inch deep in full sun once the soil has warmed, thinning to a foot or more between plants so each can branch freely. Sonja was one of the earliest branching sunflowers bred specifically for the cut-flower trade, opening a long run of 4-inch orange-gold blooms with dark centers on a compact, sturdy frame rather than one giant head. Because it carries pollen, keep cut stems out of arrangements meant for a formal table if pollen drop is a concern. Its early, reliable branching habit still makes it a benchmark against which newer garden sunflower series are often compared.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: Solar Flare Sunflower (Branching Red-and-Gold Bicolor Sunflower)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost into warm soil; stagger sowings two to three weeks apart to keep this branching bicolor flowering through late summer.

directions: Plant seed an inch deep in full sun and thin so each plant has room to send up multiple flowering side stems. Solar Flare produces 5-inch blooms with a deep red-mahogany base that flares to bright gold at the petal tips, giving each flower a glowing, two-toned look reminiscent of a sunset. Its branching habit spreads bloom over many weeks instead of a single flush, and the sturdy stems hold up well for cutting. Deadhead spent flowers regularly to keep new buds coming from lower branches.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost into deeply worked, richly amended soil; Titan needs a long, undisturbed taproot run and heavy feeding to reach its full head size.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in deeply dug, heavily enriched soil, thinning to give each plant a wide growing radius and a stout, unbranched stalk. Titan is bred for sheer scale, routinely topping 10 to 14 feet with single seed heads that can stretch well over a foot across when given steady water and monthly feeding through the season. Stake the thick stalk early since top-heavy heads are prone to wind lodging, and rotate the plant occasionally so the developing head doesn't lean permanently toward the sun. Because the heads are enormous, they double as a dramatic bird-feeding station once seeds ripen in fall.
sources: Kansas State University Research and Extension

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost along a fence line or wall that can serve as a windbreak; Sunzilla's extreme height makes it vulnerable to toppling in the open.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in fertile, well-worked soil along a sheltered spot, since this hybrid is bred to reach 15 feet or more in a single season. Sunzilla channels most of its energy into upward growth on a thick single stalk rather than a record-breaking head, making it more of a living privacy screen or novelty specimen than a cut-flower or exhibition type. Feed monthly and water deeply and consistently, since a plant this tall demands a lot of water to keep pace with its growth rate. Stake it to a post early in the season before the stalk thickens, since staking becomes difficult once the plant is established.

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost in rich, deeply cultivated soil; give this giant hybrid generous spacing so its taproot and stalk can develop without competition.

directions: Plant seed an inch deep in full sun after the soil has warmed, working aged compost into the bed beforehand to fuel this hybrid's rapid, towering growth. Paul Bunyan lives up to its folklore namesake, reliably reaching 10 to 12 feet with broad single heads on a heavy, fast-growing stalk. Keep the root zone evenly moist through the stretch of vigorous vegetative growth in midsummer, and stake the stalk while it is still young and pliable. It is a favorite for children's gardens and height competitions, and the mature heads make excellent wildlife feeders once seed has dried.

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost in rich soil with plenty of room overhead; Kong is bred for maximum height and leaf size rather than a large or early flower head.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in deeply enriched soil and water heavily through the season, since Kong is selected for outsized leaves and a stalk that can climb past 12 feet rather than for an especially large flower. The huge, coarse foliage makes it a striking temporary screen or backdrop planting, with the comparatively modest flower head appearing almost as an afterthought late in the season. Because so much of the plant's energy goes into stem and leaf growth, it benefits from monthly feeding and a stake set early before the stalk becomes too thick to support. Give it a wind-sheltered spot, as the broad leaves catch gusts that can snap an unstaked stalk.

common_name: ProCut White Lite Sunflower (Single-Stem Pale Cream Cut Flower)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil is above 60°F, and repeat sowings every 1-2 weeks through midsummer for a continuous cut-flower supply.

directions: Sow seed a half-inch deep on tight 6-to-9-inch spacing in full sun so each plant channels its growth into one unbranched, uniform stem. ProCut White Lite is the palest member of the ProCut single-stem series, opening ivory-cream petals around a dark center that reads as a soft, almost-white bloom in mixed bouquets. Like its ProCut siblings, it is bred pollen-free so it won't shed on tablecloths or other flowers, and the whole planting flowers together within a tight window for one efficient harvest. Stake rows in windy sites and cut as petals begin to unfurl for the best vase life.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: Coco Loco Sunflower (Branching Muted Rust-and-Mauve Sunflower)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost into warm soil; succession sow every couple of weeks to keep this branching, muted-tone sunflower blooming into fall.

directions: Plant seed an inch deep in full sun, thinning to leave each plant room to branch into several flowering stems. Coco Loco stands out for its unusual, low-saturation color range of dusty rust, mauve, and toasted-caramel tones with darker centers, a departure from typical bright yellow or red sunflowers that pairs especially well in muted floral designs. Its branching habit spreads bloom over several weeks rather than concentrating it into one flush, and regular deadheading keeps fresh buds coming. Cut stems hold their unusual coloring well in the vase, making it popular with floral designers seeking non-traditional palettes.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost into warm soil; Sunbeam branches from a modest height, so it suits smaller beds and cutting gardens better than full-size types.

directions: Sow seed a half-inch deep in full sun, thinning so each plant has room to send up multiple side branches. Sunbeam produces an abundance of medium-sized, clear golden-yellow blooms with dark centers on a well-branched, moderate-height plant, giving far more flowers per packet of seed than a single-headed giant. It flowers over an extended period rather than all at once, so regular cutting or deadheading keeps the display going through summer. Its manageable height makes it easier to grow without staking than taller branching types.

common_name: Pacino Gold Sunflower (Dwarf Pot and Bedding Sunflower)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost, or start indoors in cell packs 3-4 weeks early for earlier container color; Pacino Gold stays compact enough for patio pots.

directions: Sow seed a half-inch deep in full sun, or start in cell packs to transplant into containers once frost danger has passed. Pacino Gold is a deeper, richer-colored selection within the Pacino dwarf series, holding several golden-yellow blooms on a tidy, uniform plant that stays well under 2 feet tall. Its compact size and even habit make it dependable for mixed containers, window boxes, and small-space bedding where a full-size sunflower would overwhelm the planting. Deadhead spent blooms to keep new flowers forming through the summer.

common_name: Little Becka Sunflower (Dwarf Branching Red-and-Gold Bicolor Sunflower)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost, or start indoors in cell packs a few weeks early; Little Becka's small stature suits containers as well as garden beds.

directions: Sow seed a half-inch deep in full sun, thinning so each dwarf plant has room to branch. Little Becka carries the classic ringed bicolor pattern of deep red-mahogany bases fading to bright gold tips, scaled down onto a heavily branching plant that rarely tops 2 feet, so it produces a large number of small, richly colored blooms rather than one big head. The compact habit and prolific flowering make it well suited to containers, edging, and children's gardens alike. Deadhead regularly to keep the many side branches producing new buds through the season.
